notes.claim: In a shunt motor the field is across the supply, so its current and flux stay steady.
A heavier load slows the motor, which lowers the back emf, lets more armature current flow and raises the torque; the speed settles a little lower than before.
His sheet says the extra current makes the motor 'speed back up to compensate'; the fuller sources say the speed falls off as the load increases.
notes.contested: Dan's sheet says a loaded shunt motor speeds back up to compensate; textbooks say its speed is nearly constant but falls off as load increases.

notes.claim: Speed regulation is the change in speed from no load to full load divided by the full-load speed; sources differ: his sheet 10 to 20%, IDC 7 to 10%, one site puts the armature drop at about 5%.
notes.contested: Sources differ on how far a shunt motor's speed falls between no load and full load: 10-20% (his sheet), 7-10% (IDC), about 5% (a circuits site).

notes.claim: Weakening the field raises the speed: a rheostat in series with the shunt field gives speeds above rated, and is the usual method.
Start a shunt motor with the field rheostat in the slow-speed position, so the field current is at its maximum: starting torque goes with field current.
Lower starting torque than a series motor: his sheet and a text say so, while Rose-Hulman says the starting torque is as high as in the series motor.
notes.contested: Whether a shunt motor's starting torque is lower than a series motor's: his sheet and PEG-3722 say lower; Rose-Hulman says as high.

notes.claim: A shunt motor has a safe no-load speed as long as the field is not de-energised; if the field fails the speed can run away, so loss-of-field protection is usual.
Brushes and commutator need regular maintenance.
Shunt motors suit constant-speed work such as machine tools and pumps.

The supply voltage is shared between the back emf and the drop across the armature: V = Eb + Ia Ra, so Ia = (V - Eb) / Ra; the field current is a separate branch (It = Ia + If). Back emf is proportional to flux times speed.

Why the armature current follows the load: put the load on and the armature slows; the I x R drop takes a bigger share of the supply, so less back emf is needed, and the armature current and torque climb until they match the load.

Torque is proportional to flux times armature current; in a shunt motor the flux is practically constant, so torque is proportional to Ia. Speed is proportional to the supply voltage over the field flux.

Speed regulation is defined by the standard as the no-load speed minus the rated-load speed, as a percent of rated-load speed, and a dc shunt-wound motor is named as an example of a constant-speed motor.

How far a shunt motor's speed falls from no load to full load: two industry guides give 5 to 10%, his sheet gives 10 to 20%, and the armature drop alone gives about 4 to 5% (the lesson computes about 4% from the cited Rose-Hulman example). The IDC '7 to 10%' figure sits under IDC's Ward-Leonard heading (the sentence before it says the driving motor's speed is set by varying the voltage applied to the armature with a generator), so it is a figure for that system, not for a plain shunt motor on a fixed supply.
notes.contested: How far a shunt motor's speed falls from no load to full load: his sheet says 10-20%; two industry guides say 5-10%; the armature drop alone gives about 4-5%. IDC's 7-10% belongs to Ward-Leonard control, not to a plain shunt motor.

notes.claim: A cited worked example the lesson can use for its numbers: a DC shunt motor rated 600 V, 255 hp, 2000 rpm, armature resistance 0.07 ohm, total field resistance 80 ohm, drawing 353 A at rated load. The lesson computes the rest from these: field current 7.5 A, armature current 345.5 A, back emf 575.8 V, and the speed at other loads from speed proportional to back emf at constant flux (see i7.examples.json).

Whether the speed falls or rises as load goes on: the resistance drop gives a slight fall, and textbooks say so; but armature reaction weakens the flux and can make a plain 'straight shunt' motor's speed rise with load, so makers add a light series winding (stabilised shunt) to make the speed droop. His sheet says the motor speeds back up to compensate.
notes.contested: Does a loaded shunt motor's speed fall or rise? The usual rule is a slight fall; a plain straight shunt motor can rise because of armature reaction (so makers add a stabilising series winding); his sheet says it speeds back up to compensate.

notes.claim: Shunt motors suit work where the speed must stay near the set point as the load changes: pumps, fans, blowers, conveyors, machine tools and printing. The drawback noted is low starting torque.

Starting torque: a maker-neutral guide gives about 250% for a shunt machine against up to 500% for a series machine, and another says a shunt motor can deliver 300% of full-load torque for a very short time. This supports his sheet (lower than a series motor) and not Rose-Hulman's 'as high as in the series motor'.
notes.contested: Whether a shunt motor's starting torque is lower than a series motor's: his sheet, PEG-3722, MSU and Motordoc (about 250% against up to 500%) say lower; Rose-Hulman says as high.

notes.claim: Speed control in two ranges: below base speed lower the armature voltage (constant torque), above base speed weaken the field (constant power). A motor with 1750 rpm base speed on 500 V runs at 875 rpm on 250 V. Making the field stronger than rated to go slower is not allowed because the field overheats.

The field rheostat is the preferred way to adjust speed because the field current is much smaller than the armature current, so less power is lost in the rheostat; a rheostat in the armature circuit wastes more power and only lowers the speed.

Limits of field weakening: a maker winds its stock 180 V motors as plain straight shunt only for a field-weakened speed up to 105% of base speed, always keeps the speed within the maximum safe speed on the nameplate, and warns that a field-weakened motor can exceed safe speed at light load.

Starting: with no back emf at standstill only the armature resistance limits the current (a 10 hp, 0.4 ohm armature on 260 V would take 650 A, about twelve times full load); starting resistors limit it to 125 to 200 percent of full-load current. Start with the field rheostat at the slow-speed position (full field); many starters interlock the speed regulator so the motor cannot start on a weak field.
The faceplate starter: the handle is held by the no-volt coil and springs back to off if the supply fails; the overload coil short-circuits the no-volt coil on overload, so the handle is released.

Three-point and four-point starters: in a three-point starter the no-volt coil is in series with the shunt field, so it also protects against an open field; but weakening the field for speed can let the coil drop out. In a four-point starter the coil is across the supply, which frees the speed control but loses the open-field protection.

Field failure: with little or no load, losing the field supply makes the speed rise a great deal (a runaway) and damages the motor; a loss-of-field relay (device 40) is the protection named for shunt-wound DC motors, and Rose-Hulman says loss-of-field protection is usual.
notes.contested: What an open field does: with little or no load the speed runs away (MSU, Rose-Hulman, his sheet); PEG-3722 says the motor tends to keep running on residual magnetism. Both follow speed = back emf / flux: how fast depends on the load and the residual flux.

notes.claim: Residual magnetism in the poles keeps a weak field after the field winding is disconnected, and the armature keeps drawing current from the supply.
Reversing: swap either the armature leads or the field leads (not both); reversing both leaves the direction unchanged.
Lowering the field current weakens the flux, and the rotor speeds up to make the back emf the circuit needs.

Faults and tests (isolate and prove dead first): brushes and commutator are wear parts and dust collects inside; the basic checks are insulation resistance and circuit (winding) resistance; sparking at the brushes can come from the armature winding; a commutator is inspected for roughness, loose bars, uneven bar height and mica; insulation resistance of armature and field windings is covered by IEEE Std 43.

Marine and drive context: a maker lists DC motors suitable for IEEE 45 shipboard applications; a US Coast Guard specification covers DC propulsion generators and motors; shunt-wound motors pair well with SCR drives; AC drives have reduced DC machines in new large installations.

For i7 (where it is used): AC drives have taken market share from DC drives, mainly because a DC motor's brushes need regular maintenance and its commutator complicates the motor and consumes energy; a link back to lesson 3, the VSD.
